summary: This CEP Brexit Analysis briefing (No. 2, March 2016) by Swati Dhingra, Gianmarco Ottaviano, Thomas Sampson and John Van Reenen estimates how leaving the EU would affect UK trade and living standards. Using a quantitative global trade model, it finds static losses of 1.3% to 2.6% of income (£850 to £1,700 per household) after fiscal savings, and argues long-run productivity effects raise the cost to 6.3% to 9.5% of GDP. The note also covers effects on other countries, unilateral tariff removal, future trade deals, and regulation, concluding that trade losses would far outweigh EU budget savings.
one_line: CEP analysis estimating that Brexit would reduce UK income by 1.3% to 2.6% statically, and 6.3% to 9.5% with long-run productivity effects.
key_facts: The EU is the UK's largest trade partner, and around half of UK trade is with the EU.
In an optimistic scenario where the UK obtains full access to the EU single market like Norway, Brexit lowers average UK incomes by 1.3% (£850 per household).
In a pessimistic scenario with larger trade cost increases, Brexit lowers UK income by 2.6% (£1,700 per household).
The overall GDP fall in the UK is £26 billion to £55 billion, about twice the £12 billion to £28 billion income loss in the rest of the EU combined.
If the UK unilaterally removed all tariffs on imports after Brexit, UK incomes would fall by 1% in the optimistic case and 2.3% in the pessimistic case.
Including long-run productivity effects raises the cost of Brexit to a loss of 6.3% to 9.5% of GDP (about £4,200 to £6,400 per household).
The net fiscal contribution of the UK to the EU budget was estimated at around 0.53% of national income (HM Treasury, 2013).
Table 1 shows trade effects of -1.37% (optimistic) and -2.92% (pessimistic), and a fiscal benefit of 0.09% and 0.31% respectively.
The model uses WIOD data dividing the world into 35 sectors and 31 regions.
Ireland suffers the largest proportional losses from Brexit among EU members, alongside the Netherlands and Belgium.
Breinlich et al (2016) estimate that the US and Japanese trade agreements would lower prices by 0.4% and 0.2% respectively, benefits the UK would forgo outside the EU.
The UK's economy makes up only 18% of the EU's single market, reducing its bargaining power in trade negotiations.
Crafts (2016) concludes that EU membership raised UK GDP per capita by between 8.6% and 10.6%.

Booth et al (2015) identify 56 EU-derived regulations whose costs outweigh benefits, which Crafts (2016) calculates at 0.9% of UK GDP, with half the cost coming from the Renewable Energy Strategy and the Working Time Directive.
The authors state the UK already has one of the OECD's least regulated product and labour markets.
